prs.body:
## High Level Overview of Change

Removes the `XChainBridge` feature: the three ledger entries (`Bridge`, `XChainOwnedClaimID`, `XChainOwnedCreateAccountClaimID`), the eight transactors, the `STXChainBridge` and `XChainAttestations` serialized types, the RPC handling for them, and their tests — about 16.8k lines.

`XChainBridge` and `fixXChainRewardRounding` become `VoteBehavior::Obsolete`, so they can no longer be voted for. The `sfield` codes, ledger entry types, transaction types, and inner object formats they used are left marked unused so the numbers are not reassigned. The `temXCHAIN_*` and `tecXCHAIN_*` result codes are kept, since result code values must stay stable.

## Context of Change

Neither amendment was ever enabled on Mainnet, so no ledger contains these objects and no new amendment is needed to remove the code. Keeping the transactors, invariants, and 5k-line test suite alive costs maintenance on every protocol-wide refactor (`PreflightHelpers`, the autogen builders, the Beast-to-GTest migration) for a feature nobody is going to enable.

## API Impact

- [ ] Public API: New feature (new methods and/or new fields)
- [x] Public API: Breaking change (in general, breaking changes should only impact the next api_version)
- [x] `libxrpl` change (any change that may affect `libxrpl` or dependents of `libxrpl`)
- [ ] Peer protocol change (must be backward compatible or bump the peer protocol version)

`ledger_entry` no longer accepts `bridge`, `xchain_owned_claim_id`, or `xchain_owned_create_account_claim_id`. `account_objects` no longer accepts those values in `type`. `server_definitions` no longer lists the removed ledger entry types, transaction types, fields, and the `XChainBridge` serialized type. `API-CHANGELOG.md` is updated.

`libxrpl` consumers lose the `STXChainBridge` and `XChainAttestations` classes, the `keylet::bridge`, `keylet::xChainClaimID`, and `keylet::xChainCreateAccountClaimID` functions, and the `sfXChain*` fields.

## Test Plan

- `cmake --build .build` — clean.
- `.build/xrpl_tests` — 881 tests from 188 suites pass.
- `.build/xrpld --unittest --unittest-jobs 8` — 251 suites, 4857 cases, 0 failures.
- `cmake --build build/codegen --target code_gen` — no diff, the checked-in autogen headers match the macro files.
- `pre-commit run --all-files` — all hooks pass.

`Delegate_test`'s `expectedDelegableCount` drops from 56 to 48 for the eight removed delegable transactions.

reviews.author: xrplf-ai-reviewer[bot]
reviews.body: This is a large, mechanical removal of the XChainBridge feature (ledger entries, transactors, serialized types, RPC handling, and tests) plus marking the XChainBridge and fixXChainRewardRounding amendments as VoteBehavior::Obsolete. I reviewed every added (+) line across the diff — the changes are consistent: sfield/type codes and transaction numbers are deliberately left with '// N unused' comments to prevent renumbering, the Delegate_test expected count (56→48) matches exactly the 8 removed delegable transactions, the LedgerEntry.cpp dispatch simplification correctly drops the special-cased bridge/bridge_account handling now that no bridge parser remains, and the API-CHANGELOG entry accurately describes the breaking changes. One minor inconsistency worth a sanity check with the author (not a line-level bug since it only appears in deleted, not added, code): unlike sfields.macro and transactions.macro, which leave explicit '// N unused' markers for the vacated numeric codes, ledger_entries.macro removes ltBRIDGE (0x0069), ltXCHAIN_OWNED_CLAIM_ID (0x0071), and ltXCHAIN_OWNED_CREATE_ACCOUNT_CLAIM_ID (0x0074) without leaving similar reservation comments, despite the MR description stating ledger entry type numbers are 'left marked unused so the numbers are not reassigned.' Worth confirming whether that's intentional or an oversight, since it's the only place the stated pattern wasn't applied. No correctness, security, or resource-management issues found in the added code.

reviewCommentsList.body: `finalizeClaimHelper` now decrements owner counts via `adjustOwnerCount(..., {}, -1, ...)` after erasing the ClaimID SLE. comments.author: scottschurr
comments.body:
I tried signing attestations using accounts that are present in the ledger.  Then I gave the in-ledger accounts regular keys and disabled the master keys.  That works with ordinary multisigning, but is not currently working for XChain XRP transfers.

I have a unit test that reproduces the problem here: https://github.com/scottschurr/rippled/commit/5f15add691eeefde3c615f3c667148c44a755a9b#diff-b4e237ef0eaad4f10295147c159b78f2258452beb7f25b5a3256452af51a7916R800

I think this is an important test case because fixing it requires changes to the `XChainClaimAttestationBatchElement` object members.  An `XChainClaimAttestationBatchElement` currently looks like this:
```
            "XChainClaimAttestationBatchElement" : {
               "Account" : "<AccountID of source account>",
               "Amount" : "300000000",
               "AttestationRewardAccount" : "rJ8cp18RtUVDjgge6PFKDU4m9DqUN6marQ",
               "Destination" : "rGieEqubRyAuN55e2cT13XCN93MBzA5w43",
               "PublicKey" : "<public key of signer>",
               "Signature" : "...",
               "WasLockingChainSend" : 1,
               "XChainClaimID" : "1"
            }
```
Note that the the `PublicKey` and the `Account` are not related.  If the `PublicKey` isn a regular key, then you have no information for looking up the account associated with that regular key.

So I suggest that the `Account` field should be the AccountID of the signer.  That's exactly how it works for multisigning.  But we still need a field that identifies the source of the funds that are being attested to (I think that's the information we're moving out of the `Account` field). If I got that right, then consider adding an `OtherChainSource` field to the `XChainClaimAttestationBatchElement`.  The end result would look like this:
```
            "XChainClaimAttestationBatchElement" : {
               "Account" : "<AccountID of signer>",
               "Amount" : "300000000",
               "AttestationRewardAccount" : "rJ8cp18RtUVDjgge6PFKDU4m9DqUN6marQ",
               "Destination" : "rGieEqubRyAuN55e2cT13XCN93MBzA5w43",
               "OtherChainSource" : "<AccountID of source account>",
               "PublicKey" : "<public key of signer>",
               "Signature" : "...",
               "WasLockingChainSend" : 1,
               "XChainClaimID" : "1"
            }
```
That may not be the best solution and I'm very open to other ideas.  But since XChain is leveraging the existing MultiSign behavior, I think the described problem really deserves a solution.  And I'd like the solution to be as similar to preexisting multisigning as possible.

comments.author: scottschurr
comments.body:
I have a question about whether we want to disallow a bridge where `LockingChainDoor` is the same as the `LockingChainIssue::issuer`.

Here's a bridge with that configuration:
```
{
   "IssuingChainDoor" : "ra8zzeHjuHrwxAnDKHbXXoxXEe5mDxM8mq",
   "IssuingChainIssue" : {
      "currency" : "SAU",
      "issuer" : "ra8zzeHjuHrwxAnDKHbXXoxXEe5mDxM8mq"
   },
   "LockingChainDoor" : "rUR5mVQjdEH6HEvUKrcBMhZh9Rcsh45GT6",
   "LockingChainIssue" : {
      "currency" : "XAU",
      "issuer" : "rUR5mVQjdEH6HEvUKrcBMhZh9Rcsh45GT6"
   }
}
```
Note that the `LockingChainDoor` and `LockingChainCurrency:issuer` values are identical.

First, it works.  I tried it.  No problems.

But it feels funny.  If these two roles are shared, then there's nothing actually being "locked" in a documented way on the locking chain.

As is always true with an IOU, the issuer can issue an arbitrary amount.  If the issuer were only issuing on-chain, we can derive the issuer's debt by summing all trust lines associated with the currency and issuer.  And we can do that on any ledger.  So the issuer's debt is recorded (indirectly) in every ledger.

However in this case the issuer is issuing off-chain.  There is no immediate record of the issuer's debt.  Their debt could be derived by going through the metadata of all of the historical `XChainCommit` transactions with this particular Door and summing them.  But that could be a tall order.  And that does not even track funds that are returned from the sidechain.

In contrast, if the `LockingChainDoor` and the `LockingChainIssue:issuer` are _not_ the same, then there is a clear record kept on chain regarding exactly how much currency has been sent off chain.  That record is in the trust line between the door and the issuer.  So it's in a single easily identified place.  Nice.

I _like_ having that record.  And _not_ having that record makes me nervous.

So I'm wondering if we want to forbid the `LockingChainDoor` from being the same as the `LockingChainIssue:issuer`.  It would be trivial to forbid.  And we could loosen the rule later with an amendment if there were a good reason.

Thoughts?  Thanks.

## High Level Overview of Change

This pull request introduces the functionality needed to support bridging assets across ledgers. This implementation focus on connecting two XRPL-like ledgers. reviews.author: scottschurr
reviews.body:
I've finished my review.  Whew.  Most comments are inline, but there are a few notes that don't fit the inline format.  I'm leaving those here.

### Naming

I disagree with a couple of the naming choices made here.  But just because I disagree doesn't make me right.  Here are naming changes I recommend:

- I think Doors on Bridges make no intuitive sense.  Physical bridges don't have doors.  I think all three of these items (two doors and a bridge) make a Portal.  There would probably be a Portal, and LockingPortal, and an IssuingPortal, but they are all really components of the same Portal.

- I don't think you have Witnesses here, I think you have Attestors instead.  Attestors provide Attestations.


### Attestations Do Many Things

There's a problem with how many different things can happen in a single attestation batch.  One attestation batch can:

- Perform multiple payments and/or create one or more accounts.
- Add multiple attestations. None, one, some, or all of the contained attestations may be invalid.

So, conceptually, a single attestation batch may have many successful operations as well as many failed operations.  But the attestation batch only gets to return one result.

I think this conundrum deserves a special, and loud, call out in the documentation.  And it's worth being really clear about the consequences of the chosen rules.

One part of this that's really important is that _every single_ successful attestation from the batch must be added to the `ClaimID`.  Otherwise that `ClaimID` may never be successfully claimed.  If that means the every attestation batch that contains any attestations always returns  tesSUCCESS`, then that's what it takes.


### Timeouts

I think this whole thing could be made more error resilient by adding timeouts to the process of collecting attestations.  At some point we just don't expect more attestations to come in.  Once we get to that point it ought to be possible to submit a claim.  I have to admit, I've not thought through the full implementation consequences of these timeouts.  But I believe its worth figuring out.

### Unit Tests

I didn't review the unit tests.  I spent a lot of time struggling to understand them, but I didn't review them.  For me, personally, the unit test code had factored many of the important details into hard to find corners.  I was unable to understand what were, to me, important parts of the information flow given the way that the tests were written.  So I gave up and wrote my own unit tests aimed at developing my comprehension of XChain rather than test coverage.

I don't think I could do a fair job of reviewing the unit tests given the way they are structured.  I'd probably just rewrite them, which wouldn't help anybody.

I'm playing around with `XChainClaim`.  I see that the `Amount` represents the amount that will be recovered by the `XChainClaim`.  That seems fair.

However I'm seeing that the account submitting the `XChainClaim` has two things taken:

- The `Fee` and

Having the `Fee` taken is great.  That `Fee` is explicitly filled in by the account submitting the transaction.

However, having the `SignatureReward` disappear from the account took me by surprise.  There's nothing explicit in the transaction to indicate that those funds will be removed.  From what I've seen we like folks to explicitly state how much they are expecting to spend when they submit a transaction.

So my off-the-cuff suggestion would be that the `XChainClaim` transaction must contain a `SignatureReward` field that exactly matches the `SignatureReward` in the `XChainClaimID` that they are claiming.  That way the transaction explicitly identifies every amount that this transaction will cost.

Well, the `XChainClaim` tx will only succeed if a quorum of attestations is present, and those attestations do specify the reward that the `XChainClaim`  deducts from the door account (in addition to the `fee` and the `amount`), so the reward deduction should not come as a surprise. 

Also the `XChainClaim` is not strictly necessary, and the transfer can occur automatically when a quorum of attestations is reached, so you could argue that this would be even more surprising, the  `amount` + `reward` being taken from the door account without the door account submitting *any* transaction.

reviewCommentsList.author: scottschurr
reviewCommentsList.body:
I have to disagree.  It is certainly obvious that _someone_ will need to pay the `SignatureReward` for the claim.  But in the case of the `XChainClaim` it's not obvious _who_ will pay the reward.

For a normal XChain transfer I see both the `Amount` and the `SignatureReward` being paid by the door account.  That makes sense to me.  The door account explicitly signed up for the job of supplying cross-chain funds.  And the `SignatureReward` is subtracted from the `Amount`.  So only the total `Amount` moves out of the door account.

However in the `XChainClaim` case, the door account is no longer paying the `SignatureReward`.  This time it's the account that submits the `XChainClaim` transaction.  By submitting that transaction they know they are signing up to pay a `Fee`, but they may not know that they, not the door, will be expected to pay the `SignatureReward`.

Potentially the actual problem is that the door should be paying the `SignatureReward` for the `XChianClaim` (and subtracting that reward from the `Amount`), just like it does for a normal XChain transfer.  I'd be fine with that too.  But I find having the submitter of the `XChainClaim` being charged for the `SignatureReward` without explicitly saying so to be surprising.

reviewCommentsList.author: scottschurr
reviewCommentsList.body:
It looks like this code is intended to allow an attestor to sign an attestation using the Door account's master or RegularKey.  It that's what is happening I don't think that's a good idea.

The attestations are modeled after commonly used multisignatures in the XRPLedger.  You can't use the master key or regular key of the signed-for account if you use multisignatures.  You can _only_ use the multisigners in the `SignerList` owned by the account.

My strong recommendation would be to remove the code that allows a master or regular key to be used in this way.

I'm afraid that this change was the result of misunderstanding a comment I made earlier: https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/pull/4292#issuecomment-1284495909

If that's the case, then this change entirely misses the intended mark.

I've made an example of what I intended to request in https://github.com/XRPLF/rippled/pull/4292#issuecomment-1284495909.  You can see that example in the top-most commit here: https://github.com/scottschurr/rippled/commits/scottd-xbridge-reg-key

reviewCommentsList.author: scottschurr
reviewCommentsList.body:
This `!amt.native()` check allows a simple transfer of sufficient XRP (not an account creation) to create an account.  This gives XChain transfers two distinct ways to create an account:

1. With a regular claimID and cross-chain transfer of sufficient XRP.
2. With an `XChainAccountCreateCommit` transaction.

I feel like having two very different ways to achieve the same end complicates things for documentation and for users.

reviewCommentsList.author: mvadari
reviewCommentsList.body:
This is also a feature because I requested it - it's a lot easier to bootstrap a bridge when you don't need to create a temporary multisign in order to set up the initial accounts (e.g. the witness submission accounts). 

I believe the reason it was believed to be fine to do it this way is because the threat model is the same regardless - you need to trust whoever controls the account, whether that is via owning the master key/regular key or via a quorum of multisigners, since they could theoretically sign any transaction to mishandle those funds. Also, any properly set up bridge should disable the master key and should not have a regular key enabled.

reviewCommentsList.author: scottschurr
reviewCommentsList.body:
Given that we're talking about a side chain, precautions like insisting on a specific issuing account or a minimum amount of XRP in that account end up only being guidelines.  Side chains don't run the same code as the main chain.

1. It would be easy for a side chain to have a different genesis account.
2. It would be easy for a side chain to have a different starting amount of XRP.

While that's true, I don't have a strong opinion about whether any of these guidelines are retained/used.

reviewCommentsList.author: scottschurr
reviewCommentsList.body:
@mvadari, I can see how that feature add would be a convenience in certain testing scenarios.

Part of what I'm driving toward is to keep the rules and behavior for attestation handling as similar as possible to multisigning of XRPL transactions, since attestations model multisigning.  I think maintaining this kind of consistency helps users, developers, and doc folks.

>  it's a lot easier to bootstrap a bridge when you don't need to create a temporary multisign in order to set up the initial accounts

Really?  A _lot_ easier?  Setting up multisigning requires a single transaction, two transactions if you also disable the master key.  And you have to do that once for each of the two chains.  Granted, I haven't been creating test environments, so maybe I'm not seeing the actual difficulty.  But, at the moment, I'm not convinced this is a case where testing convenience should drive the design.  I'm open to being convinced, but I'm skeptical.
